title: The Maurya Empire
description: An illustrated map of the Maurya Empire, from Chandragupta’s rise after Alexander’s invasion, through Ashoka’s Kalinga war and his edicts, to its fall about 185 BCE.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Maurya Empire from about 345 to 185 BCE
note: Based on Ashoka’s inscriptions, archaeology, Greek and Latin writers, and Indian, Jain and Sri Lankan traditions written down centuries later; each chapter says which it follows. Dates are approximate and many are debated. The map is stylised and not to scale, and the empire’s borders, especially in the Deccan and the north-west, are uncertain: the areas under Powers are painted loosely. Numbers from ancient sources, such as the dead of Kalinga, are given as the sources state them.

steps.title: Magadha and the Nandas
steps.text: In the 4th century BCE the strongest kingdom in the Ganges plain is Magadha, ruled from Pataliputra, where the Son river meets the Ganga. Its Nanda kings are famous for their wealth and their huge army; Greek writers say tales of that army helped turn Alexander’s soldiers back. Later Indian stories call the last Nanda greedy and hated.

steps.title: Alexander at the Indus
steps.text: In 326 BCE Alexander of Macedon crosses the Indus. Ambhi, king of Taxila, submits, and at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) river Alexander defeats King Porus, then keeps him as an ally. At the Beas his exhausted army refuses to go further east. Alexander turns back down the Indus, leaving governors (satraps) in the Punjab.

steps.title: Chandragupta and Chanakya
steps.text: Who Chandragupta Maurya was is uncertain. Buddhist texts make him a Moriya of warrior (kshatriya) rank; some later Hindu works call him low-born. Tradition pairs him with Chanakya, a Brahmin teacher of Taxila insulted by the Nanda king, who trains the young man to overthrow him. The Greek writer Plutarch says the young Chandragupta saw Alexander.
steps.today: Today: Taxila’s ruins are a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Chandragupta takes Magadha
steps.text: Around 322 BCE Chandragupta overthrows the Nandas and takes Pataliputra, founding the Maurya dynasty. Within a few years Alexander’s governors in the Punjab are gone too; the last, Eudemus, leaves about 317 BCE. Historians debate which came first, the Punjab or Magadha, and the exact dates.

steps.title: Seleucus and the elephants
steps.text: Seleucus, one of Alexander’s generals, now rules his eastern lands. Around 305 BCE he crosses the Indus against Chandragupta. No account of the fighting survives, only the peace: Seleucus gives up Arachosia (around Kandahar) and nearby lands, receives 500 war elephants, and the two kings agree a marriage alliance whose details are unknown.

steps.title: Megasthenes in Pataliputra
steps.text: Seleucus sends an ambassador, Megasthenes, to Chandragupta’s court. His book, the Indica, is lost, but later Greek writers quote it: Pataliputra stretches about 15 km along the river, inside a timber wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Excavations at Kumhrar and Bulandi Bagh in Patna have found a great pillared hall and lines of timber palisade.

steps.title: A king becomes a monk
steps.text: Jain tradition says Chandragupta gives up his throne, follows the Jain teacher Bhadrabahu south during a twelve-year famine, and fasts to death on Chandragiri hill at Shravanabelagola. Inscriptions there, carved many centuries later, remember the story, and a cave on the hill bears Bhadrabahu’s name. Other traditions say nothing of how he died.
steps.today: Today: Shravanabelagola, Karnataka, a Jain pilgrimage site.

steps.title: Bindusara
steps.text: Chandragupta’s son Bindusara rules for about 25 years. Greek writers call him Amitrochates, from the Sanskrit Amitraghata, ‘slayer of enemies’. Little is known of his wars, but by the end of his reign the empire reaches deep into the Deccan. A Greek anecdote says he asked the Seleucid king for sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher.

steps.title: A prince in Ujjain
steps.text: Buddhist tradition says Bindusara sent his son Ashoka to put down a revolt at Taxila, then made him governor at Ujjain, capital of Avanti in central India. On the way, at Vidisha, he married Devi, a merchant’s daughter. Their children, Mahinda and Sanghamitta, would later carry Buddhism to Sri Lanka.

steps.title: Ashoka takes the throne
steps.text: When Bindusara dies, about 273 BCE, a struggle for the throne follows; Sri Lankan chronicles say Ashoka is crowned four years later. Buddhist stories have him kill 99 brothers, but this is probably legend: one of his own inscriptions mentions the households of his brothers and sisters. The stories remember the young king as ‘fierce Ashoka’ (Chandashoka).

steps.title: The Kalinga war
steps.text: Eight years after his coronation, Ashoka conquers Kalinga on the eastern coast. His own words, carved on rock, say 150,000 people were carried off, 100,000 killed and many times that number died. He writes of deep remorse. Yet that confession is left out of the edicts carved in Kalinga itself, at Dhauli and Jaugada.

steps.title: Dhamma
steps.text: Ashoka becomes a Buddhist lay follower and preaches what he calls dhamma: obedience to parents, generosity, truthfulness, kindness to servants and animals, and respect for every religious sect. He limits the killing of animals, has wells dug and trees planted along roads, and appoints officers of dhamma. His pillar at Sarnath bore the lion capital that is now India’s emblem.
steps.today: Today: Sarnath, near Varanasi; the lion capital is in the museum there.

steps.title: At the Buddha’s birthplace
steps.text: In the 20th year of his reign Ashoka visits Lumbini, where the Buddha was born, and sets up a stone pillar. Its inscription, still in place, says he freed the village from tax and cut its share of the harvest to one eighth. Found in 1896, the pillar fixed the Buddha’s birthplace.

steps.title: Edicts in Greek and Aramaic
steps.text: At Kandahar, on the empire’s western edge, Ashoka’s words were carved in Greek and Aramaic for local readers; the inscriptions were found in 1958 and 1963. His edicts name five Greek kings to whom he sent envoys, among them Antiochus II of Syria and Ptolemy II of Egypt. Dhamma appears in Greek as eusebeia, ‘piety’.

steps.title: Words on the rock
steps.text: Fourteen of Ashoka’s major edicts are carved on a great boulder at Girnar, in Gujarat. The same rock carries a Sanskrit inscription of about 150 CE recording repairs to the nearby Sudarshana lake, which it says was built under Chandragupta and given channels under Ashoka. Most of the edicts are in Prakrit, written in the Brahmi script.

steps.title: Mahinda in Lanka
steps.text: Sri Lankan chronicles say Ashoka’s son Mahinda, now a monk, comes to Lanka and converts King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale, near Anuradhapura. His sister Sanghamitta, a nun, brings a cutting of the bodhi tree under which the Buddha found enlightenment. A tree in Anuradhapura said to grow from it is still honoured.

steps.title: The southern edicts
steps.text: Minor edicts at Maski, Brahmagiri and other sites in Karnataka mark the empire’s southern edge. Beyond it the edicts name independent peoples, the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras, to whom Ashoka sends medical care for people and animals. The Maski edict, found in 1915, was the first to name the king as Asoka.

steps.title: Ashoka’s last years
steps.text: Buddhist tradition says Ashoka gave so much to the Buddhist order (sangha) that his ministers and grandson stopped him, until all he had left to give was half an amalaka fruit. It also places a great Buddhist council at Pataliputra in his reign. He dies about 232 BCE, after ruling for some 36 years.

steps.title: The empire divides
steps.text: After Ashoka the sources disagree. The Puranas list several kings with short reigns. Jain texts praise his grandson Samprati, linked with Ujjain, as a great patron. Another grandson, Dasharatha, left inscriptions dedicating caves in the Nagarjuni hills near Gaya to Ajivika ascetics. Kashmir and the north-west seem to break away under other princes.
steps.today: Today: the Nagarjuni caves are beside the Barabar caves, Bihar.

steps.title: Greeks in the north-west
steps.text: Around 206 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III crosses the Hindu Kush and renews friendship with an Indian king, Sophagasenus, who gives him elephants; who this king was is unknown. From about 180 BCE Greek kings of Bactria, starting with Demetrius I, push into Gandhara and the Punjab.

steps.title: The last Maurya
steps.text: The last Maurya king, Brihadratha, is killed by his own commander, Pushyamitra Shunga, while reviewing the army; the story comes from the 7th-century CE writer Bana, and the Puranas agree that Pushyamitra took the throne. His Shunga dynasty rules a smaller kingdom from Pataliputra and Vidisha. The Maurya Empire, some 140 years old, is over.

steps.title: Ashoka rediscovered
steps.text: For centuries no one could read Ashoka’s inscriptions. In 1837 James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script. The edicts’ ‘Devanampiya Piyadasi’, Beloved of the Gods, was linked to Ashoka through the Sri Lankan chronicles, and the Maski edict confirmed it in 1915. India adopted the Sarnath lion capital as its emblem in 1950; Ashoka’s wheel is on its flag.
steps.today: Today: Ashoka’s wheel (chakra) is at the centre of India’s flag.

items.name: Seleucid Empire

facts.Founder: Seleucus I, one of Alexander’s generals

items.role: The Greek kingdom to the west, which trades land, envoys and gifts with the Mauryas.

Antiochus II is named in Ashoka’s edicts
Antiochus III receives elephants from an Indian king, Sophagasenus (about 206 BCE)

items.name: Kalinga
items.role: A coastal kingdom outside the empire until Ashoka conquers it, about 261 BCE.

items.name: Southern kingdoms
items.role: Independent kingdoms beyond the southern border. Ashoka names them as neighbours and sends them medical help and his dhamma.

items.name: Anuradhapura kingdom
items.role: The Sri Lankan kingdom that, by tradition, receives Buddhism from Ashoka’s son Mahinda.

items.name: Greco-Bactrian kingdom
items.role: Greek kings of Bactria who push into north-west India from about 180 BCE, as Maurya power fades.

items.name: Shunga dynasty
items.role: Founded by the general who kills the last Maurya, it rules a smaller kingdom in the Ganges plain and central India.

items.name: Chandragupta Maurya
items.role: Founder of the Maurya Empire
items.text: Chandragupta rises from uncertain origins to rule from Afghanistan to Bengal; Greek writers call him Sandrokottos. He takes Magadha from the Nandas, drives out Alexander’s governors and makes peace with Seleucus. Jain tradition says he ends his life as a monk at Shravanabelagola.

items.name: Chanakya
items.role: Brahmin adviser to Chandragupta, in tradition
items.text: Also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta, Chanakya is remembered as the cunning minister who made Chandragupta king. The Arthashastra, a treatise on running a state, is credited to him, though scholars think it was compiled and revised over later centuries. The Greek writers who knew the court do not mention him.

items.name: Alexander of Macedon
items.role: King of Macedon
items.text: Alexander conquers the Persian Empire and reaches the Indus in 326 BCE. After defeating Porus he wants to march on to the Ganges, but his army refuses at the Beas. He dies in Babylon in 323 BCE, and his generals divide his empire.

items.name: Seleucus I
items.role: One of Alexander’s generals; founder of the Seleucid kingdom
items.text: Seleucus wins Alexander’s eastern lands, from Syria to Bactria. Unable to recover the Indus lands, he makes peace with Chandragupta, trading territory for 500 elephants. The elephants help him win the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE against his rival Antigonus.

items.name: Megasthenes
items.role: Seleucid ambassador to Chandragupta’s court
items.text: A Greek diplomat who lives at Pataliputra, Megasthenes writes the Indica, the fullest early foreign account of India. It survives only in quotations by later writers such as Strabo and Arrian. He describes seven classes of society and city officials, though some of his stories, such as gold-digging ants, are fanciful.

items.name: Bindusara
items.role: Second Maurya emperor
items.text: Son of Chandragupta and father of Ashoka. Few records of his reign survive, though Greek writers knew him as Amitrochates and Seleucid envoys came to his court. Buddhist texts say he favoured the Ajivikas, a sect of ascetics. By his death the empire covers most of the subcontinent.

items.name: Ashoka
items.role: Third Maurya emperor
items.text: His inscriptions call him Devanampiya Piyadasi, ‘Beloved of the Gods, of gracious looks’. After the bloody conquest of Kalinga he turns to Buddhism and to dhamma, and has his ideas carved on rocks and pillars across his empire. Buddhist tradition remembers him as the ideal king.

items.name: Mahinda
items.role: Buddhist monk; Ashoka’s son, in tradition
items.text: The Sri Lankan chronicles make Mahinda the son of Ashoka and Devi, ordained as a monk at about 20. He leads the mission that brings Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and Sri Lankans remember his arrival each year at the Poson festival.

items.name: Sanghamitta
items.role: Buddhist nun; Ashoka’s daughter, in tradition
items.text: Ordained as a nun when her brother becomes a monk, Sanghamitta travels to Lanka with a cutting of the bodhi tree and founds an order of nuns there, according to the Sri Lankan chronicles. She is remembered on the full moon day of Unduvap.

items.name: Pushyamitra Shunga
items.role: Maurya commander who founds the Shunga dynasty
items.text: As commander of the army, Pushyamitra kills the last Maurya and takes the throne. Later Buddhist texts accuse him of persecuting Buddhists, which some historians doubt. A later inscription credits him with two horse sacrifices (ashvamedha), a claim to great royal power.

items.name: James Prinsep
items.role: Scholar and assay master of the Calcutta Mint
items.text: Working in Calcutta, Prinsep deciphers the Brahmi script and helps crack Kharosthi, unlocking Ashoka’s inscriptions and early Indian coins. He reads the edicts in 1837, shortly before illness sends him back to England, where he dies in 1840.
